title: Immunization and Spot Rates
text:
Duration
\[D = \sum_{t} t \cdot \frac{CF_t / (1+y)^t}{P}\]
The present-value-weighted average time to receipt, in years.
For a zero-coupon bond, \(D\) equals maturity. For a coupon bond, \(D\) is less than maturity.

title: Immunization and Spot Rates
section: Modified duration and the price approximation
text:
Modified duration and the price approximation
\[D^* = \frac{D}{1+y}, \qquad \frac{\Delta P}{P} \approx -D^* \times \Delta y\]
A bond with \(D = 7\) and \(y = 4\%\) has \(D^* = 6.73\). A 100 basis point rise in yields gives
\[\frac{\Delta P}{P} \approx -6.73 \times 0.01 = -6.73\%\]

title: Immunization and Spot Rates
text:
Definition
A portfolio of bonds is immunized against a liability when two conditions hold at the same time:


Present value
\[PV_{\text{assets}} = PV_{\text{liability}}\]


Duration
\[D_{\text{assets}} = D_{\text{liability}}\]


Portfolio duration is the value-weighted average of the durations of the holdings.

title: Immunization and Spot Rates
section: What the two conditions do and do not deliver
text:
What the two conditions do and do not deliver


Holds
Small parallel shifts, immediately after the match is struck.


Surplus
Large parallel shifts, when asset convexity exceeds the liability’s.


Deficit
Non-parallel shifts, and the passage of time, since durations drift apart.


Rebalancing is required as time passes and as rates move.

text:
What each one reports


Income statement
Revenues and expenses over a period, on an accrual basis.


Balance sheet
Assets, liabilities, and equity at a point in time. Two consecutive balance sheets give the change in working capital.


Cash flow statement
Cash received and paid over a period, split into operating, investing, and financing.

title: From Statements to Free Cash Flow
text:
The definition
\[\text{FCFF} = \text{EBIT}(1-t) + \text{D\&A} - \text{CapEx} - \Delta \text{NWC}\]
Cash generated by operations after reinvestment, before any payment to debt or equity holders.

title: From Statements to Free Cash Flow
text:
Two routes to one number


From the income statement
\(\text{EBIT}(1-t)\)
\(+\ \text{D\&A}\)
\(-\ \text{CapEx}\)
\(-\ \Delta \text{NWC}\)

From the cash flow statement
\(\text{Cash from operations}\)
\(+\ \text{Interest}(1-t)\)
\(-\ \text{CapEx}\)

Equal only after reconciling non-cash items.

title: From Statements to Free Cash Flow
text:
Why they disagree


Non-cash charges you forgot
Stock compensation, impairments, deferred taxes.


Working capital, redefined
The cash flow statement’s version is not the balance sheet’s.


Leases
Operating lease treatment changes both EBIT and capital expenditure.


Acquisitions
Reinvestment reported separately from capital expenditure.

title: Course Overview
text:
Best practices — structure


Every assumption gets its own labeled cell, in one block at the top
Formulas reference those cells, never a number typed inside the formula
The same formula runs across every period of a projection
Every hardcoded number carries its source beside it



Write =B5*(1+$B$6), not =B5*1.05. Source format: document, date, specific reference — “Company 10-K, FY2025, page 45, revenue note.”

title: Course Overview
text:
Best practices — presentation







Convention
Rule




Blue text
Hardcoded inputs — the cells a reader is meant to change


Black text
Every formula and calculation


Green text
Links to another sheet in the same workbook


Currency
Dollar sign, commas, no decimals: $1,234,567


Units
Stated in the header, not in every cell: Revenue ($mm)


Percentages
One decimal: 12.4%. Valuation multiples as 8.5x


Negatives
In parentheses: (123), not −123



Zero formula errors on delivery: no #REF!, #DIV/0!, #VALUE!, or #NAME?.

title: Course Overview
text:
Why the colors matter


The color convention is not decoration. It is how a reader knows, at a glance, what they are allowed to change.


For your reader
Blue says “this is an assumption, argue with it.” Black says “this follows from the assumptions, do not touch it.”

text:
What is running there


The harness
Claude Code, connected to GLM 4.7 — a capable and relatively inexpensive model from Z.ai.


The software

The screen

title: Course Overview
section: Three things that will trip you up
text:
Three things that will trip you up


Refresh
The file browser does not notice a new file on its own. Use the refresh button above it.


No Excel in the lab
Office is not installed. Double-clicking a workbook there does nothing.


Download to open
Workbooks come down to your laptop through the three-dots menu, and open in your own Excel.

title: Course Overview
section: The large language model (LLM) only writes text
text:
The large language model (LLM) only writes text

The model cannot open a file, run a calculation, or fetch a filing. It reads text and writes text. That is the entire capability.

What makes it useful is the harness around it. The model emits a request to use a tool; the harness runs the tool and reports the result back.

title: Course Overview
text:
The loop


The harness sends the prompt, the conversation, and the list of tools
The model answers: use tool X, with these arguments
The harness runs X and reports the result back
The model decides what comes next — another tool, or an answer for you



On the lab, GLM writes a Python file, runs it at the terminal, reads the output, and revises. Four tool calls before you see anything.

title: Course Overview
text:
What that produces


Excel workbooks
Written cell by cell with Python: inputs as numbers, formulas as formulas.


Charts and figures
Any chart style, custom annotations, labels, fonts


Word and PowerPoint
Real files with editable text, not pictures of them.


Data analysis
Data fetched, merged, filtered, aggregated — statistics and regressions


Advanced data analysis
Simulations, optimizations, machine learning


Web apps
A page someone else can use, from a description of what it should do.

title: Course Overview
text:
Example
Try this prompt:

Build an Excel workbook containing a mortgage amortization table. Put the loan amount, rate, and term in labeled input cells at the top. Include a chart of the amount going to interest and the amount going to principal each month.

title: Course Overview
text:
What comes back




The workbook
Inputs in labeled cells, an outputs block below them, 360 rows of schedule.
The selected payment cell holds =$B$12, not 2,528.27.
Change the rate and the whole sheet recalculates.

title: Course Overview
section: And the chart it asked for
text:
And the chart it asked for


A chart object bound to the cells, not a picture pasted in. Change the rate and the crossover moves with it.

title: Course Overview
text:
Claude inside Excel

There are also Claude, ChatGPT, and CoPilot plugins for Excel , from Home → Add-ins. The chat window sits inside the workbook.



They need paid accounts or particular types of license agreements. We will not use them.

title: Course Overview
text:
Plan before you act
For any complex operation, ask AI to plan first, or ask it what the best way is to do something, before it begins to work.


Planning pulls the knowledge in
Plan how you will do this before you start. The plan puts the relevant considerations into the conversation, and it answers in light of those rather than from base rates.


Planning breaks the work up
Steps you can check one at a time. Failures stay small and local instead of surfacing at the end, when everything downstream is already wrong.

title: Course Overview
text:
Misunderstandings and bad assumptions


The problem
Errors usually come from

AI misunderstood what you wanted, or
The task could be done in multiple ways, you did not specify, and AI chose the wrong path



What to say:

Tell me what you are about to do
Tell me what you did
Was there any ambiguity in my instructions? Did you make any choices we did not discuss?

title: Course Overview
text:
Numbers need code

AI has gotten better at arithmetic, but it is still not to be trusted at math — it is trained to predict language
Always ask it to run code if you need a number
It may not be good at predicting what should follow “what is 32 times 17?” but it is very good at generating code “x = 32 * 17; print(x)”

title: Course Overview
section: Ask why your idea is bad, not why it is good
text:
Ask why your idea is bad, not why it is good
Training on human feedback teaches that agreement earns high ratings. Ask “is this valuation sound?” and it will find reasons that it is.

Invert it. What is the strongest argument that this project should be rejected?

title: Course Overview
text:
Use independent agents as critics


AI is not a good self-critic
Ask AI in the same conversation to evaluate its work. It will review its own reasoning and conclude it is sound.


Start a new conversation or ask for a subagent
A new conversation or a subagent will not see the prior reasoning. It will look at it “with a fresh set of eyes.”

title: Course Overview
text:
Hallucinations

Hallucinations are much less frequent now than a few years ago
Hallucinating code is really not an issue
Ask for web search and a source for any fact
The greatest risk is asking for an obscure fact that it cannot find via a web search

title: Course Overview
text:
Verify and retain code


Check the outputs
We don’t usually check AI code by reading it. We check small cases where we can verify “by hand” (using AI to help with that too).


And keep what works
Keep code that has been vetted. Tell AI to use it again the next time.

This afternoon

Five cases and two short ones. Read, argue, build, defend.



The pattern

What is being graded

What are we comparing this against?

The floor space

Northeast corner, building two

What did you charge, and what would you say to someone who charged nothing?
Is your charge the same in every year? Should it be?

The nine operators

Quintero and Baig are looking at the same nine people. What is each of them claiming?
What would have to be true about Tannehill for Baig to be right? For Quintero?
The case tells you several things about the grinding department. Which of them carry weight, and why?
What did you assume, and how much of your answer rests on it?

title: Capital Budgeting
section: The old machines, and the rebuild that never happens
text:
The old machines, and the rebuild that never happens

Tannehill can sell the three old machines. How much does that actually improve year zero?
Two of the manual cells need rebuilding in year four if they stay in service. Does that belong in this analysis? Where?
Which assumption in your model would you want to verify before committing the money, and how would you verify it?

title: Capital Budgeting
text:
Takeaways


A project is a comparison
Name the counterfactual before you name a number: what happens if we don’t do it?


Opportunity cost
Not zero because you own it, and not the accounting charge. It is the cash the resource would earn in its next best use.


Allocations are averages
Charge the project what changes. Sometimes that is less than the allocation. Sometimes it is more.

title: Bond Pricing and Duration
section: A bond is a promise with a date on it
text:
A bond is a promise with a date on it


Coupon
Fixed cash on fixed dates. Contractual, not discretionary.


Principal
Face value, repaid at maturity.


Yield
Not a promise. The rate that makes today’s price equal the discounted promises.

title: Bond Pricing and Duration
text:
One rate is not enough
\[P = \sum_{t=1}^{T} \frac{C}{(1+r_t)^t} + \frac{F}{(1+r_T)^T}\]
Each cash flow is discounted at the rate for its own maturity. The set of rates \(r_1, \ldots, r_T\) is the term structure.

title: Bond Pricing and Duration
section: Lab 1 — price one off the curve
text:
Lab 1 — price one off the curve
Spot rates for maturities 1 through 10 are on the handout.


Lay out the ten cash flows of a 10-year 4% annual coupon bond
Discount each at the spot rate for its own maturity, and sum
Find the single yield that produces the same price



Report the price and that yield.

title: Bond Pricing and Duration
text:
Interest rate risk
A bond’s price falls when yields rise. The size of the fall depends on the timing of the cash flows, not on maturity alone.
A 10-year 8% coupon bond returns cash earlier than a 10-year zero, and its price moves less for the same change in yield.

title: Bond Pricing and Duration
text:
Duration
\[D = \frac{\sum_t t \cdot w_t}{\sum_t w_t}, \qquad w_t = \frac{CF_t}{(1+y)^t}\]
The average date on which you get your money, weighted by present value.
\[\frac{\Delta P}{P} \approx -\frac{D}{1+y} \times \Delta y\]

title: Bond Pricing and Duration
text:
Lab 2 — predict, then check


Compute the bond’s duration from the same spreadsheet
Predict the price change for a 100 bp rise, using \(-D^* \times \Delta y\)
Reprice at the higher yields and compare



Post two numbers: the predicted price change and the actual one.

title: Bond Pricing and Duration
text:
Accuracy of the approximation
The formula is a first-order approximation: it uses the slope of the price-yield relation at the current yield.
The price-yield relation is convex, so the actual price exceeds the linear estimate for both increases and decreases in yield. The error grows with the size of the yield change.

The proposal

text:
Ten percent, or thirty-five

What is Sethi claiming about who buys fresh dog food? What is Petrosyan claiming?
What evidence does each of them have, and how good is it?
How would you settle this, and could it be settled before the money is spent?

title: Capital Budgeting
section: What goes in, and what stays out
text:
What goes in, and what stays out

Kestrel has already spent on consumer research and formulation. How does that enter your model?
Corporate charges the line for overhead at a percentage of revenue. How does that enter?
When kibble sales are lost to the fresh line, what exactly does Kestrel lose?
Compare your three answers with the person beside you. Where do you differ?

title: Capital Budgeting
text:
Working capital, and the equipment

The line ties up working capital as it grows. How did you handle that?
The equipment is seven-year property and the committee is looking at five years. How did you handle the mismatch?
What happens to the equipment at the end, and what does that do to the tax bill?

title: Capital Budgeting
section: The number that ends the argument
text:
The number that ends the argument

Your NPV moves with the cannibalization rate. At what rate would you be indifferent?
What does having that number do to the argument in the room?
What would change your mind about which side of it Kestrel sits on?
What should the capital committee do when it meets on the eighteenth?

title: Capital Budgeting
text:
Takeaways


Sunk costs
Money already spent does not enter the analysis.


Cannibalization
When a project takes revenue from an existing product, the loss is that product’s cash flow.


Allocations are averages
Charge the project what changes — which is sometimes less than the allocation and sometimes more.


Working capital is a change
You fund the increase, not the level, and you get it back at the end.


Tax schedules outlive projects
A depreciation schedule set by statute does not stop when your forecast does. The gap is what makes a disposal taxable.


Find the threshold
A breakeven turns an argument about beliefs into a question about evidence.

title: Capital Budgeting
text:
And one more

Dunmore Brewing · two minutes

Dunmore launches a hard seltzer at $40 million of revenue. Research says 60 percent of the volume comes out of a competitor’s seltzer, 15 percent out of Dunmore’s own light lager, and 25 percent is new to the category. The light lager carries a 44 percent contribution margin.

How much should Dunmore charge the seltzer project for cannibalization?
Should Dunmore be pleased or worried that most of the volume comes from a rival?

title: Capital Budgeting
text:
Eight minutes

Before we start on Kinnaird

Ivara distributes packaged food to convenience stores from one leased warehouse. Cost accounting charges each product line $14.00 per pallet shipped. A proposed frozen line would ship 40,000 pallets a year, so the model carries a $560,000 annual warehouse charge.
The warehouse is full. It has been at capacity for two years. The frozen line would go into third-party overflow space at $0.90 million a year.

What does the frozen line actually cost Ivara in warehouse space?
How does that compare with what the model carries?
Would your answer change if the warehouse had room to spare?

title: Capital Budgeting
text:
Takeaway

An allocation bundles costs that behave differently. Occupancy here is fixed and does not respond to the decision; handling is variable and does. Striking the allocation whole is as wrong as keeping it whole, and as wrong as swapping it for the market price of one of its parts. The work is to take it apart.

Read

title: Capital Budgeting
text:
Rasch’s memo

Rasch’s arithmetic checks out. Do you agree with his conclusion?
His annual saving is the same figure in year 1 and in year 15. What is that saying about the world?
Where does his discount rate come from, and is it the right rate for these cash flows?

title: Capital Budgeting
text:
Both ways

There is more than one internally consistent way to build this project. What are they?
Build it both ways. What do you expect of the two answers before you look?
If they do not agree, how would you go about finding out why?

title: Capital Budgeting
text:
What does not inflate

Which cash flows in this project rise with inflation, and which do not?
How did you treat the service contract? The depreciation deductions?
Is there a rule in this you could hand someone building their next model?

title: Capital Budgeting
text:
What it means more generally

Gas is expected to rise faster than prices generally. What does that mean for the savings in real terms?
Suppose inflation ran well above expectations for fifteen years. Who would win and who would lose on a project like this?
Rasch wrote “revisit if gas moves.” What would you send back to him?

The project in nominal terms, escalating what escalates
The same project in real terms, agreeing to the dollar
Rasch’s version alongside, for the difference
The gas price at which the project fails

title: Capital Budgeting
text:
Takeaways


Market rates are nominal
A discount rate built from observed yields and premiums already contains expected inflation. It cannot be paired with cash flows that do not.


A flat price is a forecast
Holding a number at today’s level is a claim that the real price falls every year.


Consistency, not preference
Real and nominal both work and must agree to the dollar. Only the mixture is wrong.


Divide, do not subtract
The real rate is the nominal over inflation, minus one. The shortcut is close at 2 percent and far off at 40.


Some amounts are fixed in nominal terms
Signed contracts, statutory deductions, fixed-rate debt, dollar covenants. In a real model, each of them has to be deflated.


Inflation and the depreciation shield
Depreciation is set in the dollars of the purchase date and deducted in later, cheaper ones. Higher inflation lowers the real value of the shield, which matters most for capital-intensive projects.

title: Capital Budgeting
text:
Takeaways


A future choice is not a forecast
You do not forecast what you will do. You value the right to decide later, with information you do not have now.


Value at the node, then discount
Work backward. Take the maximum at each decision date, and carry that back.


Order matters
Take expectations before the decision and you have assumed the decision is made without knowing which state occurred.


The two options differ in size
Expansion pays off in the states where cash flows are high. Abandonment pays off in the states where they are low.


They are one distribution
As success becomes likelier the expansion right grows and the abandonment right shrinks. They are not two values to add together.


When staging is worth paying for
If you are confident, build everything rather than pay to keep the decision open.

title: Capital Budgeting
text:
Takeaways


A point estimate is a distribution
A single column states that every input is known.


The base case is not the mean
The value at the average input is not the average value. Wherever the model multiplies uncertain things together, the two differ.


One at a time is not uncertainty
Moving each input alone holds every other input at its base value. Things that go wrong tend to go wrong together.


Correlation is a claim
It is an assertion about what drives the business, and it comes from people who know the industry, not from the model.


Pick the statistic deliberately
The mean, the median and the fifth percentile answer different questions. Report the one that matches the consequence you face.


Something chose the defaults
Every model contains assumptions nobody made on purpose.

title: Capital Budgeting
text:
Twelve minutes
Ivara distributes packaged food to convenience stores from one leased warehouse. Warehouse cost is collected in a pool and charged to product lines at $14.00 per pallet shipped — $5.60 of occupancy, $8.40 of handling labor and equipment.
A proposed dry goods line would ship 40,000 pallets a year, so the model carries a $560,000 warehouse charge. The warehouse has been full for two years and the lease is fixed. The line’s inventory would go to a third-party facility, 3,000 pallet positions at $210 a position, worked by Ivara’s own crews.

Occupancy of the existing building: when, and how much?
Third-party space: when, and how much?
Handling labor: when, and how much?
What should the line be charged for warehousing?
Would your answer change if the warehouse had room to spare?
